paragraphs.notes: CR-12.26 changes one word: 'As long as the corn and wine held out' -> 'As long as the grain and wine held out'. CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: Butler's five clauses all survive. They are the month of south and east wind; the men sparing the cattle while the corn and wine held out; hook and line and bird-catching once the ship's food was gone; Odysseus going inland to pray; the hand-washing, prayer and sleep. Every clause except the second is byte-identical to the accepted BEFORE and to the previously verified successor 862066e2, so only the one word is in play. FIDELITY: Butler's 'corn' is the British generic word for cereal grain, and 'grain' is its exact present-day equivalent. The Greek is Od. 12.327, οἱ δ᾽ εἷος μὲν σῖτον ἔχον καὶ οἶνον ἐρυθρόν, 'as long as they had sîtos and red wine'. σῖτος is grain, especially wheat, and the bread or food made from it, so 'grain' is faithful to Butler and to Homer. Homer's 'red' is already absent from Butler, so it is not a package loss. 'held out' is Butler's own verb, meaning lasted or remained in supply. It is kept, as D29 prefers, where LIVE paraphrases 'lasted'. 'As long as the grain and wine held out' is natural current English, and the article 'the' is BEFORE's. The meaning that the provisions lasted carries straight into the next sentence, 'when they had eaten everything there was in the ship' (12.329, νηὸς ἐξέφθιτο ἤια πάντα). Nothing is added, lost or glossed. The agent, the sequence and the concessive 'hungry as they were' are untouched. NECESSITY (class 8): the change is needed. For a present-day American reader, the edition's audience under the GLOSSARY spelling standard, 'corn' means maize. 'corn and wine' aboard a Homeric ship therefore pictures a New World crop, a silent anachronism the reader has no cue to correct. This is the package's own Book 3 ruling, and B24-03 applied the same reasoning at 24.20. The edit also completes consistency: the other seven Butler 'corn' sites all print 'grain' in AFTER. Leaving 'corn' would regress LIVE, which already prints 'grain' here. COLLISION (D26): Butler's ¶26 has no 'grain'. AFTER ¶26 has exactly one, and it renders Butler's single 'corn'. No two Butler words are merged, and 'everything there was in the ship' is untouched. In the neighbouring paragraphs, which are outside D26's paragraph scope, 'grain' fits rather than collides. ¶25's 'meat and drink' is Butler's idiom for βρῶσίς τε πόσις τε (12.320), food and drink. ¶28's 'no barley left' (κρῖ, 12.357–358) names a kind of grain, so the stores visibly run out, where 'corn' would have set maize against barley. There is no new ambiguity: 'grain' among a ship's provisions cannot be read as the unit of weight or as wood grain. CONVENTIONS AND GRAMMAR: American usage. No GLOSSARY row is overridden, because GLOSSARY.md has no corn or grain entry. There is one opening “, the running-speech convention of Odysseus's narration, with counts identical to BEFORE. No ASCII quotes, no 'towards', no dashes, no double spaces. Grammar is sound. REASON CHECK: the citation is accurate. book03-continuity.md lines 268–269, under B03-P037 (the sheet's IDs are 1-indexed, so this is 0-based 3.36), reads: '"corn lands" → "grain lands" — British corn means grain, and an American reader reads maize.' The reason quotes it word for word, with a colon for the em dash and without the markdown emphasis. The sîtos gloss is tied to 12.327 by its line reference and is correct there. It also holds at 13.7, 13.22, 17.53 and 20.27. The remaining sites translate other Greek: 3.36 is πεδίον πυρηφόρον, 'wheat-bearing plain'; 20.16 is ὑποσταχύοιτο; 24.20 is Butler's reading of διατρύγιος. That is immaterial, because the ruling concerns Butler's English word. Provenance is confirmed: out/book24-verify.json (round 2) records 12.26 as an out-of-scope observation, and screening/consistency-corn.json matches the edit-list entry field for field, plus severity 'recommended'. 'Ten flagged Books' matches the screening set 3–10, 23 and 24; Book 12 is outside it.

LIVE 12.26 reads: For a whole month the wind blew steadily from the south, with no other wind except south and east. As long as grain and wine lasted, the men didn't touch the cattle when hungry. But when they had consumed everything on the ship, they were forced to roam farther, catching birds with hooks and lines and taking whatever they could find, for they were starving. One day I went inland to pray to heaven to show me some means of escape. When I had gone far enough to be away from all my men and found a place well sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the Olympian gods until they sent me into sweet sleep. CENSUS: BUTLER has whole-word 'corn' 8 times, once each at 3.36, 12.26, 13.7, 13.22, 17.53, 20.16, 20.27 and 24.20. None is in a title, and the only other corn- words are corner and cornice. AFTER prints 'grain' at all eight and has no whole-word 'corn' anywhere. For comparison, BEFORE had 'corn' at 12.26 and 24.20, 862066e2 at 12.26 only, and LIVE at 24.20 only. AFTER 12.26 has exactly one 'grain', and Butler's 12.26 has none. CONVENTIONS in AFTER 12.26: typographic quotes (one opening “, as in BEFORE), no ASCII quotes, no 'towards', no spaced dashes, no double spaces. All pass. PACKET: the BEFORE, AFTER and context texts match the files verbatim, and BUTLER matches the served original after whitespace normalization. VERDICT: 1 of 1 VERIFIED CLEAN, 0 defects. The edit is faithful: Butler's British 'corn' means grain, and the Greek is σῖτος at Od. 12.327. It is necessary, because American 'corn' means maize. It follows the package's Book 3 ruling (citation accurate, continuity lines 268–269) and all seven other sites. It creates no collision and keeps Butler's 'held out'. OVERALL: VERIFIED CLEAN.
